body.text: This page on the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) sets out Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive framework for corporations, individuals, trusts and partnerships filing Form T661 with the Canada Revenue Agency, where Part 8 confirms advisory tool review. The key takeaway: eligible work must be a systematic investigation seeking scientific or technological advancement, supported by contemporaneous evidence.

As of November 2026, Canada's federal R&D tax landscape has undergone its most substantial legislative expansion in over a decade. Under Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government enacted major enhancements retroactively effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. These enacted reforms double the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds), broaden the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extend the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out test (which Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations may also elect to use), and restore the eligibility of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Furthermore, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval program (Form T1322) offering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks, and Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) has proposed expanding SR&ED to include regulatory certification and intellectual property (IP) protection commercialisation costs. At the provincial level, Québec's 2025–2026 Budget replaced its legacy R&D tax credit suite with the unified, 100% refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (30% on the first $1,000,000 above the exclusion threshold and 20% on excess expenditures) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, while British Columbia's 2026 Budget made its 10% credit permanent and fully harmonized with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration.
1. Statutory & Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure under the Income Tax Act

Canada's primary federal mechanism for supporting industrial and academic research and development is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, established under the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "ITR"). Unlike discretionary grant programmes that operate under fixed budgetary appropriations, the SR&ED program is an entitlement-based statutory tax incentive administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance, conducts claim reviews, and issues tax assessments and cash refunds.

The program delivers financial support to qualifying taxpayers—corporations, individuals operating sole proprietorships, beneficiaries of trusts, and members of partnerships—through a two-stage statutory mechanism under the ITA. First, under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may accumulate allowable current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and—for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—allowable capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the taxpayer (or a related corporation under subsection 37(1.1)) in a pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Deductions from the Section 37 expenditure pool are optional in any given taxation year; any undeducted positive pool balance does not expire and may be carried forward indefinitely to reduce net business income for tax purposes in future taxation years, subject to loss restriction event rules upon an acquisition of control under subsection 37(6.1). By exception, a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance to a subsequent fiscal period and must fully deduct the pool in computing partnership net income in the year incurred under paragraph 96(1)(e.1).

Second, under subsection 127(5) and the definitions in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, taxpayers earn an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their SR&ED qualified expenditure pool. Under section 127.1 of the ITA, qualifying claimants with insufficient federal Part I tax payable may receive a partial (40%) or full (100%) cash refund of their unused current-year ITCs. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax otherwise payable.

To prevent double dipping between the income deduction and the tax credit, paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA link the two incentives across consecutive taxation years. Any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax payable or refunded in cash in a given taxation year (excluding ITCs allocated from a partnership) reduces the taxpayer's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year (reported on Line 435 of Form T661). If this reduction causes the Section 37 expenditure pool balance to become negative at the end of that subsequent taxation year, the negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(v), effectively making used and refunded ITCs subject to income tax in the taxation year following their utilization or refund.
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which generally conforms to the OECD Frascati Manual. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" that falls into one of three core categories, supplemented by eligible support work and bounded by seven statutory exclusions.

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research is defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view—for example, studying a newly discovered virus in a laboratory solely to understand its molecular characteristics and expand the scientific knowledge base. Under paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research is defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view—such as investigating how to develop a vaccine against a newly discovered virus by exploiting its identified molecular characteristics. Under paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development—which accounts for the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada—is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto (such as attempting to generate new technological knowledge during the scale-up and optimization of processes to enable rapid, large-scale vaccine manufacturing).

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), SR&ED also encompasses support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Support work is never SR&ED in isolation; to qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), it must be both commensurate with the needs (corresponding in amount, size, extent, or duration necessary) and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the ITA explicitly exclude work undertaken with respect to seven specific operational and commercial activities from constituting SR&ED, even if carried out by scientists or engineers:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes; and
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection.

body.text: In distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) from excluded work under paragraphs (e) through (k)—such as eligible experimental data collection versus excluded routine data collection—the CRA's guidelines emphasize that the decisive factor is the purpose of the activity. If data collection or testing is performed specifically to test a hypothesis in an SR&ED investigation, it qualifies as support work; if it is conducted for normal commercial operations or quality assurance, it is excluded. Furthermore, activities related to acquiring knowledge or know-how that already exists—including employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring experts or consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—do not attempt to achieve a scientific or technological advancement and cannot be claimed. Under subsection 37(4) of the ITA and paragraph 2902(c) of the ITR, no SR&ED deduction or ITC is allowed for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED.
1.3 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From the Five Questions to the Two-Requirement ("Why" and "How") Framework

The CRA's administrative guidance for evaluating whether work satisfies subsection 248(1) has evolved through several distinct historical phases. Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada relied on Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, which taxpayers found insufficient to clarify the boundaries of eligible development. Following the May 1985 Budget Papers—which introduced the statutory term "experimental development" to exclude routine engineering—and a March 4, 1986 clarification from the Department of Finance, Revenue Canada and industry leaders published Information Circular IC 86-4 (later revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994), establishing three core criteria: scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content.

In 1998, Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada delivered the landmark ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520 (TCC), synthesizing the concepts of IC 86-4R3 with subsection 248(1) into five judicial criteria. The CRA subsequently codified Justice Bowman's five questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012 and revised on April 24, 2015) as a two-step methodology: Step 1 asked the Five Eligibility Questions—(1) Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty? (2) Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty? (3) Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis? (4) Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement? and (5) Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?—while Step 2 determined the extent of eligible work by separating support work from excluded work.

On August 13, 2021 (modified July 5, 2022), the CRA archived the 2015 Eligibility of Work Policy and replaced it with the modernized Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While both the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) and the binding judicial authority of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain completely unchanged, the 2021 Guidelines consolidated the five questions into a two-pillar "Why" and "How" Requirement Framework:

cells: 1. The "Why" Requirement (Purpose: Scientific or Technological Advancement)
The work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement.

Focuses on generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (theories, prediction models, causal relationships) rather than purely factual knowledge (routine measurements or data).Triggered by a scientific or technological uncertainty—when it is unknown whether a given result or objective can be achieved due to an insufficiency or gap in the available scientific or technological knowledge base (considering both internal business resources and publicly available knowledge).Seven indicators of insufficient technological knowledge in experimental development: (1) existing design methods are not applicable; (2) requirements/specifications do not conform to existing standards; (3) too many variables or unknowns; (4) parameters/conditions lie outside the normal operating range; (5) problem nature is continuously evolving; (6) data is not readily available; or (7) interlocking constraints exist.Success or failure is irrelevant: Learning through testing that a hypothesis is not a viable solution still advances technological knowledge.
2. The "How" Requirement (Methodology: Systematic Investigation or Search)
The work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis.

Following normal design methods, established protocols, or routine systematic problem-solving is insufficient.Step 1: Defining the problem / scientific or technological uncertainty.Step 2: Generating a hypothesis (an idea consistent with known facts as a starting point for resolving the uncertainty).Step 3: Planning and testing the hypothesis through experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively as testing progresses.Step 4: Developing logical conclusions based on the testing findings.Step 5: Keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

body.text: In framing claims on Form T661, the CRA Guidelines distinguish between a broad company project—which encompasses commercial objectives such as launching a product line or expanding a facility—and an SR&ED project, which typically exists as a subset within the company project and comprises the interrelated activities collectively necessary to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainty. An SR&ED project starts when the scientific or technological uncertainty is identified (technical feasibility studies qualify only if followed by experimentation or analysis testing a hypothesis) and ends when the advancement is achieved or the uncertainty is determined to be unresolvable. Routine troubleshooting, debugging, fine-tuning without new technological uncertainties, customer installation, and beta testing to verify specifications fall outside the SR&ED project duration. Where experimental development is conducted in an active commercial manufacturing facility ("Shop Floor SR&ED"), claimants must apply the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (updated July 19, 2016) and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (updated July 19, 2016) to isolate eligible experimental runs from excluded commercial or excess production under paragraph 248(1)(i).
1.4 Landmark Legislative Reforms (2024–2026): From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15 and Budget 2026
When auditing or preparing Canadian SR&ED claims for the 2024 through 2027 taxation years, practitioners must carefully distinguish among three sequential stages of federal legislative reform.
Stage 1: The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 2024) & August 15, 2025 Draft Legislation

In pre-announcements on December 13, 2024, and the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), followed by draft legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, the federal government initially proposed four foundational reforms effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. First, the FES proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000 (which would have yielded a maximum refundable ITC of $1,575,000). Second, it proposed raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for CCPCs from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000. Third, it proposed extending the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average consolidated gross revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), while allowing CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue phase-out structure. Fourth, it proposed restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024.
Stage 2: Federal Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) & Enactment via Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

In the 2025 Federal Budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, the federal government confirmed all the 2024 FES measures and further increased the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from the initially proposed $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. These measures were formally enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. As a result, the legacy $3,000,000 expenditure limit applies only to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the interim $4,500,000 FES proposal was superseded prior to enactment, and the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (providing up to $2,100,000 annually in refundable federal ITCs) is the binding statutory law for all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
Stage 3: Federal Budget 2026 Commercialisation Proposals (Tabled November 5, 2026)

In Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny, tabled November 5, 2026), the federal government announced that rather than introducing a separate patent box regime, it proposes to expand the SR&ED program to include specific commercialisation expenses incurred in taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day (November 5, 2026). Projected in the Budget 2026 fiscal tables to deliver $930 million in federal tax relief over five years ($25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million ongoing in 2030–2031), the Budget 2026 proposals encompass two new areas:

items: Regulatory and Certification Requirements: Eligible activities would expand to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialise a product or process, provided these activities directly relate to a project that is eligible under existing SR&ED rules. The claimable expenditure categories remain the same as standard SR&ED rules (wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead costs, and machinery and equipment).

Intellectual Property (IP) Protection Costs: Eligible expenditures would expand to cover expenses reasonably incurred to prepare and file an application to register IP protection, as well as periodic maintenance costs required to keep IP rights in force, for IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project. Eligible forms of IP protection are patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software under relevant Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign legislation. While administrative fees paid to an IP office outside Canada would qualify, supporting activities (such as preparing an application) would be eligible only if conducted in Canada. Costs incurred to enforce IP rights (such as infringement litigation) or costs not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP rights are excluded. Furthermore, if a taxpayer disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was provided for IP protection costs, recapture rules will apply to recover the related SR&ED deduction and ITC amounts.

2. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Caps, Refundability & Carryover Rules
2.1 Basic vs. Enhanced Investment Tax Credit Rates
Under section 127 of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), the federal SR&ED ITC operates on a two-tier volume-based rate structure.

The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35% is available to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) (and their eligible Canadian-resident subsidiaries) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit ($6,000,000 maximum for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3,000,000 maximum for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, when only CCPCs qualified).

The Basic (General) ITC Rate of 15% applies to four categories of claimants and expenditures: (1) all corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and non-qualifying public corporations) on 100% of their qualified SR&ED expenditures; (2) qualified SR&ED expenditures of a CCPC or ECPC that exceed its annual expenditure limit; (3) individuals (sole proprietorships) and beneficiaries of trusts; and (4) partners of a partnership, where the ITC is calculated at the partnership level under subsection 127(8) strictly at the 15% basic rate, even if individual partners are CCPCs.
2.2 Corporate Classifications: CCPCs, Qualifying Corporations, Excluded Corporations, and ECPCs

Because both the ITC rate (35% versus 15%) and the cash refundability rate (100%, 40%, or 0%) depend on the claimant's statutory classification, tax auditors must verify four corporate definitions under subsections 125(7), 127(9), 127.1(2), and 248(1) of the ITA.

A Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) is a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (encompassing both de jure voting control and de facto operational or economic control under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by one or more corporations listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination of them.

Within the CCPC category, the refundability provisions in subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA distinguish among three sub-types of CCPCs: (1) a Qualifying Corporation (other than an Excluded Corporation), which is a CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable income of all associated corporations) does not exceed its qualifying income limit—defined in the CRA SR&ED Glossary as $500,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is ≤$10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess of taxable capital over $10,000,000; (2) an Excluded Corporation; and (3) an Other CCPC (other than a qualifying or excluded corporation). While the 2019 federal budget eliminated prior-year taxable income from the calculation of the expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced rate, this sub-classification among CCPCs still dictates whether the corporation receives a 40% cash refund or 0% refund on its 15% above-limit ITCs (and whether an excluded corporation is limited to a 40% refund on its 35% up-to-limit ITCs).

An Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—created by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—is defined under subsection 127(9) of the ITA as a corporation that meets three conditions throughout the taxation year: (1) it is resident in Canada; (2) a class of its shares is listed on a designated stock exchange (or it has elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) it is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. The non-resident control test includes a statutory aggregation rule: even if all the shares of the corporation owned by non-residents were instead owned by a single hypothetical person, the ECPC must still not be controlled by that hypothetical person. Additionally, Canadian-resident subsidiary corporations where all or substantially all (90% or more) of the issued shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC.
2.3 Annual Expenditure Limit & Phase-Out Formulas (Pre- and Post-December 15, 2024)

The annual expenditure limit caps the amount of qualified SR&ED expenditures on which a CCPC or ECPC can earn the enhanced 35% ITC. Associated CCPCs (under section 256 of the ITA) must share a single annual expenditure limit by filing Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit); if the associated group fails to file Schedule 49, the CRA sets the expenditure limit to nil. Similarly, members of a consolidated corporate group of ECPCs must share a single expenditure limit across the group. Short taxation years (fewer than 51 weeks / 365 days) and multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year proportionally reduce the expenditure limit.

For taxation years beginning BEFORE December 16, 2024, only CCPCs qualify for the 35% enhanced rate, and the maximum annual expenditure limit is $3,000,000. Following the 2019 federal budget, the $3,000,000 limit is reduced solely based on the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated group. The phase-out begins at $10,000,000 and reaches nil at $50,000,000 (a reduction of $0.075 for every $1 of taxable capital above $10,000,000):

Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤$10,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess of that taxable capital over $10,000,000

For taxation years beginning AFTER December 15, 2024, both CCPCs and ECPCs qualify for the 35% enhanced rate, and the maximum annual expenditure limit is $6,000,000 (increased from the $4,500,000 interim figure proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement by the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget and enacted in Bill C-15). The phase-out thresholds have been broadened to start at $15,000,000 and reach nil at $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out band, corresponding to a reduction rate of $0.10 per $1 of excess under the enacted $6,000,000 limit, or $0.075 per $1 under the earlier $4,500,000 draft FES proposal):

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤$15,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of that taxable capital over $15,000,000

For an ECPC—or for a CCPC (or associated group of CCPCs) that elects to determine its expenditure limit using gross revenue instead of taxable capital—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (or consolidated group's) average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years (as reported in GAAP annual financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation, regardless of whether group members were associated throughout the entire 3-year period) exceeds $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated at $75,000,000:

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − B) ÷ $60,000,000, where B is nil if average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years is ≤$15,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of that average gross revenue over $15,000,000

As PwC and tax practitioners highlight, this election allows each CCPC to select whichever phase-out metric (prior-year taxable capital or three-year average gross revenue) produces the higher expenditure limit—providing major relief to pre-revenue or early-stage R&D companies with >$15,000,000 in paid-up equity/debt capital but low gross revenues.

3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods & Cost-Reduction Rules

To claim SR&ED tax incentives on Form T661, a taxpayer must link its eligible technical projects to its allowable SR&ED expenditures (Part 3, Section B of Form T661), compute its pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (Part 3, Section C), and then calculate its total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Part 4).
3.1 Election of Overhead Calculation Method: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Under subsections 37(8) and 37(10) of the ITA and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a claimant must elect either the Proxy Method (Form T661, Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Form T661, Line 162) for each taxation year. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that year.

Actual overhead costs are not specifically identified or claimed on Form T661 (they remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under s. 9(1) ITA). Instead, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible salary base (Part 5, Line 820 of Form T661). body.text: Under the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated April 28, 2022 / March 27, 2026) and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, the PPA rate has been 55% of the salary base since 2014 (following a transition from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013). Under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, the salary base used to compute the 55% PPA for any employee (whether a specified employee or a regular arm's length employee) must exclude: (1) taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the ITA; (2) bonuses and remuneration based on profits; (3) employer-paid related payroll benefits; and (4) unpaid amounts from a prior taxation year paid in the current taxation year and reported on Line 310 of Form T661.

Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) of the ITR, the PPA is constrained by an Overall PPA Cap so that the PPA, qualified SR&ED expenditures, and specified non-SR&ED tax deductions do not exceed total business deductions claimed in computing net business income for the year:
Overall PPA Cap = A − B − C

where A is the total amounts deducted in calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold), B is the sum of deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED pool deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development), and 104 (trusts) of the ITA, and C is the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building. If a taxpayer carries on more than one business, the specified deductions across all businesses must be aggregated.
3.2 Salaries or Wages & Specified Employee Restrictions

Under subsections 37(8) and 248(1) of the ITA, subsection 2900(2) of the ITR, and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), eligible salaries or wages consist of employment income from an office or employment (excluding superannuation/pension benefits, retiring allowances, employer-paid related benefits, extended vacation or sick leave, and stock option benefits granted on or after November 17, 2005) attributable to the portion of time employees spend directly engaged in SR&ED. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" is a question of fact based strictly on the hands-on technical tasks performed, not the employee's job title. Qualifying duties include preparing equipment and materials for experiments (excluding routine maintenance), carrying out experiments, tests, or analyses, performing eligible support work, and first-line technical supervision that directly influences the technological course of ongoing SR&ED. Work above first-line supervision, non-technological management decision-making, and clerical/administrative tasks (accounting, payroll, HR, purchasing, sales, legal support) are not considered directly engaged. If an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of their working time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages counts (subsection 2900(5) ITR); otherwise, only the documented percentage of SR&ED time is eligible.

For regular (non-specified) employees, allowable SR&ED salaries or wages on Line 300 include base pay, vacation/holiday/sick pay, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, inducements/non-competition payments, cash outlays for taxable benefits, and qualifying non-cash taxable benefits (provided the value is a reasonable estimate of actual cost, excludes recoverable GST/HST/PST, and is not deducted elsewhere as a business expense)—although bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits are excluded from the Part 5 PPA salary base.

Under subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2) of the ITA, a claimant may also claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada (reported on Line 307 for regular employees and Line 309 for specified employees of Form T661), provided two strict conditions are met: (1) the foreign SR&ED work is directly undertaken by employees of the claimant (foreign subcontractors and foreign branches do not qualify), and (2) the foreign work forms an integral part of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant. Total permissible foreign SR&ED salary or wages in a taxation year is capped at 10% of the total salary or wages for SR&ED carried on inside Canada (10% of Line 306 on Form T661), and the amount claimed for specified employees on Line 309 cannot exceed 10% of Line 306 minus the amount claimed for regular employees on Line 307.
Strict Statutory Restrictions for "Specified Employees"

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a specified employee is an employee who is a specified shareholder—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time during the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of a related corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse, child, sibling, or parent of a controlling shareholder, even if that relative owns zero shares). Under the ITA ownership attribution rules, shares held by related persons are attributed to the employee, shares held through partnerships or fixed trusts are counted proportionally, and beneficiaries of a discretionary family trust are treated as owning 100% of the trust's shares. Holding ≥10% of any class of shares at any point in the taxation year renders the individual a specified employee for that period, even if their ownership is subsequently diluted below 10%.
If an employee is a specified employee, three strict statutory limits apply to their remuneration:

items: Zero Eligibility for Bonuses and Profit-Based Pay (Subsection 37(9) ITA): Any bonus (an amount paid in addition to normal pay, including common owner-manager year-end bonus declarations to reduce corporate income) or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is completely excluded from SR&ED expenditures (earning $0 in SR&ED deductions and $0 in ITCs).

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap of 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1) ITA): The maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages (Line 305 of Form T661) that may be claimed for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. Under subsections 37(9.2) to (9.4) of the ITA, associated corporations employing the same specified employee must share a single 5 × YMPE cap and file an allocation agreement on Form T1174; if they fail to file Form T1174, none of the specified employee's salary counts in any of the associated entities.

Proxy Salary Base Cap of Lesser of 75% of Total Salary and 2.5 × YMPE (Subsections 2900(7) and (8) ITR): When calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method (Part 5 of Form T661), the salary base for a specified employee cannot exceed the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year late-paid wages)—meaning that even if a founder spends 100% (ASA) of their time on SR&ED, their proxy salary base is still capped at 75% of their total salary; and (b) 2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year (2.5 × YMPE × days employed in the taxation year ÷ 365), shared across associated corporations.

3.3 The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration & Unpaid Expenditure Rules
Auditors must verify compliance with two separate 180-day payment rules governing accrued liabilities at year-end.

First, for unpaid salary or wages, subsections 78(4) and 127(26) of the ITA mandate that any salary or wages accrued at year-end must be physically paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year (payment on the 180th day is timely, and timely remittance of CPP/source deductions is the CRA's primary proof of payment). If accrued salary or wages remain unpaid after the 180th day, the unpaid amount is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year for either the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool or the qualified expenditure pool for ITCs (reported as unpaid on Line 315 of Form T661). Instead, it is deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (claimed on Line 310 of Form T661 in the year paid). However, under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, late-paid prior-year salary reported on Line 310 is permanently excluded from entering the Part 5 proxy salary base, permanently forfeiting the 55% PPA on that remuneration. (Reasonable vacation or holiday pay and amounts under a statutory salary deferral arrangement are deemed paid on the 180th day for direct salary claims, though excluded from the PPA salary base.)

Second, for unpaid current expenditures other than salary or wages (such as materials, arm's length contracts, or overhead), subsection 127(26) of the ITA provides that amounts unpaid 180 days after the taxation year-end still enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the year incurred, but must be deducted when calculating qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (Line 520 of Form T661) in that year, and are added back to qualified expenditures (on Line 500 of Form T661; at 80% for arm's length contracts/third-party payments) in the subsequent taxation year when paid.
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and (B)(V) of the ITA, paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR, and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated December 18, 2014 / March 27, 2026), material costs are claimable under both the Proxy Method and Traditional Method only when they are physical, tangible substances or items (solid, liquid, or gaseous) that compose the body of a tangible thing at a given moment in the SR&ED process. Intangible items, data, software licences, equipment, utilities (gas, propane, electricity), and reusable laboratory glassware or supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, test tubes, pipettes, filter papers, solvents, acids, lubricants, cleaning supplies) do not qualify as SR&ED materials, although reusable laboratory supplies and incremental utilities may qualify as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are physically consumed or transformed in SR&ED in Canada (not when purchased into inventory), and their laid-down cost includes invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, third-party preparation services (such as galvanizing metal parts prior to destructive testing), and—for internally manufactured inventory—direct materials, direct labour, and a share of manufacturing production overhead (even under the Proxy Method).

The CRA distinguishes between Materials Consumed (Form T661, Line 320)—which are destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (such as chemicals, growth media, seeds, or test boxes destroyed during trials, which are never subject to ITC recapture)—and Materials Transformed (Form T661, Line 325), which are changed or incorporated into another product, prototype, or commercial asset that retains residual or commercial value. If transformed materials are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the ITC Recapture Rules (subsections 127(27) to (36) of the ITA) apply to recover the ITC earned on those materials.

3.6 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from SR&ED deductions and ITCs. Effective for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024) and lease costs incurred/first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restored capital eligibility under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026 / June 24, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026).
All or Substantially All (ASA) Capital Property (Paragraph 37(1)(b) ITA; Form T661, Line 390)

Depreciable property (property for which Capital Cost Allowance could otherwise be claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a) of the ITA, excluding land, inventory, goodwill, buildings, or leasehold interests in buildings, other than prescribed special-purpose buildings approved by the Department of Finance) acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant satisfies the intent test to either: (1) use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, OR (2) consume ASA (≥90%) of its value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF—desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators; importantly, computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are NOT GPOEF and therefore qualify) is excluded.

An SR&ED capital expenditure deducted from the Section 37 pool in a year is deemed to be claimed as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), so it must not be duplicated on Schedule T2SCH8. Crucially, while both new and used ASA depreciable property enters the Section 37 pool for 100% immediate income deduction (Line 390), used equipment (property that was used or acquired for use or rent for any purpose before acquisition by the claimant) is a prescribed expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR that must be deducted on Line 532 of Form T661—meaning only new capital property qualifies to earn SR&ED ITCs.

Regarding the exact effective-date transition, while the general coming-into-force rule of Bill C-15 applies to property acquired after December 15, 2024, tax specialists at Scitax Advisory Partners note that subsection 127(11.2) of the ITA (as amended by Bill C-15) contains a specific deeming rule for ITC purposes: "expenditures incurred to acquire property described in paragraph 37(1)(b) are deemed not to have been incurred before the property is considered to have become available for use by the taxpayer, determined without reference to paragraphs 13(27)(c) and (28)(d)". Consequently, Scitax notes a technical argument that if new R&D equipment (such as an environmental chamber) was ordered, paid for, and delivered prior to December 16, 2024, but was not hooked up, commissioned, and "available for use" until after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(11.2) deems the expenditure to be incurred on the post-December 15, 2024 available-for-use date for ITC purposes—though claimants are cautioned that the CRA may challenge this interpretation or Finance Canada may propose clarifying amendments.
First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) ITA; Form T661, Line 504)

If new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, does not meet the ≥90% ASA intent test, is not GPOEF, and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the ITR (which excludes property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life, or used in the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility, plant, or line, such as a $20,000,000 commercial pulp-mill boiler undergoing commissioning trials), it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under both the Proxy and Traditional Methods based on its actual SR&ED operating time:

items: First-Term SUE: Actual SR&ED operating time in Canada is primarily (>50%) of total operating time during the first period, which starts when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 12 months after that date. Qualifies for an ITC on 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (claimed on Line 504 / Box 792 of Form T661 in the taxation year in which the first period ends).

Second-Term SUE: Must have qualified as First-Term SUE, and actual cumulative SR&ED operating time in Canada must remain primarily (>50%) during the second period, which starts when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 24 months after that date. Qualifies for an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost on Line 504 (for a combined maximum of 50% of the capital cost across both terms).

3.7 Overhead, Cloud Computing, Software & Prescribed Exclusions (Regulation 2902)

Under the Traditional Method, overhead and other expenditures claimed on Line 360 must satisfy the cumulative two-part test in paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the ITR and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022): they must be (1) directly related (having a direct linkage without an intervening step to the SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or SR&ED machinery) and (2) incremental (would not have been incurred if the SR&ED prosecution had not occurred; flat headcount percentage allocations of general corporate expenses are disallowed).

Under this framework, utilities (electricity, gas, water) that vary directly with the operation of SR&ED machinery qualify proportionally; travel and lodging in Canada for employees directly performing, supervising, or supporting SR&ED trials at a customer or supplier site qualify; technical training in Canada directly linked to SR&ED work qualifies (whereas administrative training is excluded); and moving expenses to relocate SR&ED candidates or employees within Canada qualify (whereas headhunter fees, job advertising, interview travel, and work-permit/immigration costs are excluded from SR&ED and deductible only as ordinary business expenses). Fixed monthly telephone, cell phone, and Internet subscriptions are disallowed as non-incremental, though specific incremental long-distance charges qualify. For cloud computing, dedicated telecommunications bandwidth, and software, the Tax Court of Canada held in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877 (TCC), that leasing dedicated lines/bandwidth and external mainframes constitutes an equipment lease rather than general overhead. With the post-December 15, 2024 restoration of capital and lease expenditures under Bill C-15, scientific and engineering software licences, computer workstations, and leased equipment/servers used ASA (≥90%) or primarily (>50%) for SR&ED in Canada are once again claimable.

Regardless of whether the Proxy or Traditional Method is chosen, Regulation 2902 of the ITR excludes prescribed expenditures from qualified expenditures (deducted on Lines 530 and 532 of Form T661), including: (1) fees for preparing SR&ED claims; (2) legal or accounting fees (including patent legal fees prior to the proposed Budget 2026 expansion); (3) interest and financing costs; (4) dues or fees for membership in a scientific or technical society; (5) convention or conference attendance costs; (6) entertainment, advertising, or selling costs; (7) fines or penalties; (8) used equipment (for ITC purposes); and (9) expenditures to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED.
3.8 Government Assistance, Contract Payments & the 20-Year ITC Recapture Rules

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the ITA and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, SR&ED tax incentives are provided strictly on the claimant's net SR&ED costs. Any government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable or conditional loans from federal, provincial, municipal, or foreign governments or public authorities—such as NRC IRAP, SADI, CEWS, or provincial/territorial R&D tax credits, excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself), non-government assistance (inducements or reimbursements included under paragraph 12(1)(x)), or contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date for the taxation year reduces both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Lines 429–432) and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes (Lines 513–518) on a project-by-project basis. Under the Proxy Method, however, because overhead is not in the deductible pool, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit attributable to the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount does not reduce the federal SR&ED pool or qualified expenditures; instead, that PPA portion is included directly in taxable income in the year received or applied against tax. When a claimant repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED pool, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool (Line 445) and earns ITCs in the year repaid.

Under subsections 127(27) to (36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 14, 2022), if a taxpayer acquired SR&ED property (materials transformed, ASA capital property, SUE, or physical components purchased under an arm's length SR&ED contract) in the current year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36)), earned an SR&ED ITC on that property, and subsequently sells/disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the taxpayer must add an ITC Recapture Amount directly to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion:
ITC Recapture Amount = lesser of (a) the ITC earned in respect of the property and (b) the ITC rate that applied to the original expenditure × Base Value

where the Base Value is the Proceeds of Disposition (for an arm's length sale) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property at the time of conversion to commercial use or non-arm's length disposition (for SUE, multiplied by 25% for First-Term SUE or 50% for Second-Term SUE). Notably, if a component is purchased from an arm's length supplier for $12,000, the full $12,000 is subject to recapture upon commercial conversion; whereas if the component is manufactured in-house, the in-house salaries and overhead used to build it are exempt from recapture. Any ITC recaptured and added to Part I tax payable in a year increases the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).

4.2 Complete Suite of Prescribed Federal SR&ED Forms & Updated Form T661 (26)

On Form T661 (26) (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), Part 1 captures general claimant details. Part 2 (Project Information — Lines 200 to 282) requires technical narratives and project-level information for the claimant's 20 largest projects by dollar value (while Part 2 descriptions for all other claimed projects must still be completed and retained in the claimant's records). Updated Form T661 (26) introduces several new lines in Part 2: Line 207 requires the 5-digit CRDC Field of Research Code (RDF#####) from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0; Lines 212 and 214 capture whether Pre-Claim Approval was obtained (Line 212) and the assigned Pre-Claim Approval Case Number (Line 214); Line 242 describes the scientific or technological uncertainties; Line 244 describes the systematic investigation, hypotheses, and testing performed in the taxation year; Line 246 describes the scientific or technological advancements achieved; Lines 262 and 263 require listing the names of up to 10 of the most expensive depreciable SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024, claimed on Line 390 (Line 262) and the percentage of total operating time used in SR&ED for each property (Line 263); and Lines 270 to 282 require checking the specific contemporaneous supporting documentation maintained for the project. (If a federal agency has designated a project as "classified information" for national security reasons, Section B of Part 2 is completed on a separate sheet retained by the claimant while a notification letter is filed with Form T661.)

Part 3 of Form T661 (Lines 160 to 470) records the irrevocable method election (Line 160 Proxy vs. Line 162 Traditional), allowable current expenditures (Lines 300–380), restored SR&ED capital expenditures on Line 390, total allowable expenditures (Line 400), and the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool continuity (Lines 429–470). Part 5 (Lines 800 to 820) computes the salary base and 55% PPA, Part 6 allocates project costs, Part 7 provides statistical data, and Part 8 confirms advisory tool review.

Part 9 of Form T661 (Claim Preparer Information) mandates full disclosure of whether a third-party claim preparer participated in preparing the claim, including the preparer's Business Number, billing arrangement code (e.g., contingency fee rate), and total fees. Even if no external claim preparer was engaged, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA, if prescribed information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed, for which both the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable (though an omission limited to Part 9 does not disallow the underlying SR&ED claim).
4.3 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval program, enabling qualifying businesses to obtain an upfront written determination from the CRA on whether their planned projects meet the statutory definition of SR&ED before commencing work or incurring major costs. To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business must: (1) operate in Canada as a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership; (2) have less than $25,000,000 in annual gross business income; and (3) be in good standing with the CRA. Each submitted project must represent new or recently begun work not included in a prior SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under objection or litigation.
The Pre-Claim Approval application and review process follows five sequential steps:

items: Request a Case Number on Canada.ca: The business submits an online web form providing its contact details and 15-character Business Number. Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing receive a case number via My Business Account within 2 business days; new SR&ED claimants receive a phone call from the CRA within 5 business days.

Complete Form T1322 (Maximum 3 Projects): Using the assigned case number, the applicant completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval) for up to 3 projects. Section B of Form T1322 requires three technical responses: Line 042 (what scientific or technological uncertainty the project aims to address, maximum 500 words), Line 043 (what due diligence was completed—such as literature searches, patent reviews, or initial trials—to confirm the uncertainty cannot be resolved using existing knowledge, maximum 700 words), and Line 044 (what systematic investigation, hypotheses, and experiments are planned over the up-to-3-year period, maximum 900 words).

Upload Application & Supporting Documents in My Business Account: In a single online session under "Correspondence -> Submit documents" using the case number, the business uploads signed Form T1322 along with up to 10 supporting documents (project planning documents/Gantt charts, description of planned internal time-tracking and record-keeping controls, due diligence references, and project team credentials).

Meet with the Assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): A virtual or on-site meeting with the RTA (estimated duration 2 to 5 hours) is mandatory for new claimants and optional at the RTA's discretion for existing claimants in good standing.

Receive Written Determination Within 8 Weeks (Valid up to 3 Years): Within 8 weeks of receiving the complete application, the CRA issues a Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report. If granted, the approval is valid for up to 3 years (unless material changes occur, which should be reported to the RTA). While the business must still file Form T661 after performing the work (entering the case number on Lines 212 and 214), claims containing only pre-approved projects that are selected for review receive an expenditure-only review with the processing service standard cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. (There is no formal objection or appeal process if pre-claim approval is denied, though the claimant may still submit a regular Form T661 claim after undertaking the work.)

body.text: 4.4 The CRA Audit & Review Process, Service Standards, Penalties & Dispute Resolution

Under subsection 230(1) (keeping books and records) and section 231.1 (inspecting and requesting information) of the ITA, as detailed in the CRA Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025 / April 20, 2026), all filed SR&ED claims undergo automated and manual risk assessment. Once a claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn, because Form T661 is an irrevocable part of the income tax return. Furthermore, as confirmed in Ludco Enterprises Ltd. v. M.N.R., 93 DTC 1351, The Queen v. McKinley Transport Ltd., 90 DTC 6243, and AGT Ltd. v. Canada, 97 DTC 5189, CRA reviewers have legal authority to expand the scope of a review to additional projects or issues and to inspect documents whose relevance can only be determined upon examination.

Reviews are conducted (primarily via virtual videoconference, or on-site on an exceptional basis) by a coordinated two-person team: a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), who evaluates technical eligibility under subsection 248(1), interviews the claimant's technical leads, authors the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, and reports to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM); and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who verifies payroll, time sheets, contracts, overhead, and assistance, and reports to a Financial Review Manager (FRM). The CRA's service standard for processing refundable SR&ED claims selected for full review is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (90 calendar days for expenditure-only reviews of pre-approved claims; non-refundable claims do not have a fixed service standard).

If the CRA determines during a review of an initial or amended return that a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (where the CRA bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities under subsection 163(3)), made or participated in a false statement or omission, the CRA assesses a Gross Negligence Penalty under subsection 163(2) (paragraphs 163(2)(a) and (d)) of the ITA and the Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025). The penalty is equal to the greater of $100 and 50% of the total of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (treating overstated pool deductions and overstated ITCs as deducted first, and deeming loss-year taxable income not to be less than zero under subsection 163(2.1)), plus (2) the entire overstated refundable ITC refund claimed.

When the RTA and FR issue a draft proposal package proposing negative adjustments or penalties, the claimant is granted 30 calendar days to submit written representations and supporting evidence. If disagreements persist, the claimant may escalate through informal dispute resolution to the RTM and FRM (including requesting a joint meeting) before the reassessment is finalized. Once a formal Notice of Assessment or Notice of Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 calendar days from the date on the notice to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, and may subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine of Canada's ten provinces and one of its three territories offer provincial or territorial R&D tax credits; only Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not have a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA via schedules filed with the T2 corporate return (or T1 individual return in Newfoundland and Labrador and Yukon).

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal ITA, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (unless formally renounced/waived by the filing due date where permitted, and excluding the portion attributable to the 55% federal Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method) constitute government assistance that reduces the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 429) and the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool (Lines 513 and 514) before the 35% or 15% federal ITC is computed.
5.1 Québec: The New CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025) vs. Legacy R&D Credits

In its 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, the Government of Québec enacted a sweeping reform of its innovation tax assistance system under the Taxation Act (Loi sur les impôts, R.S.Q., c. I-3), administered by Revenu Québec.
The New Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) — Taxation Years Beginning After March 25, 2025

Effective for corporate taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec consolidated and replaced four major tax credits—(1) the R&D Salaries and Wages Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.7-V), (2) the University/Public Research Centre Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), (3) the Pre-Competitive Private Partnership Research Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and (4) the Industrial Design Tax Credit—and abolished four other measures: (5) the Research Consortium Fees and Dues Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V), (6) the Technological Adaptation Services Tax Credit, (7) the Five-Year Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers, and (8) the Five-Year Tax Holiday for Foreign Experts.

In their place, Québec introduced the single, unified Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization / Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation (CRIC). Unlike the legacy regime—which differentiated rates by corporate asset size (30% for SMEs versus 14% for large corporations)—the CRIC is 100% refundable for all eligible businesses regardless of size and modulates its rate solely by expenditure volume above an annual exclusion threshold:

items: 30% fully refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T); and
20% fully refundable rate on all eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures beyond $1,000,000 above the exclusion threshold, with no upper expenditure ceiling.

body.text: Crucially, the CRIC expands eligible activities beyond traditional SR&ED to include pre-commercialisation activities—such as technological validations, regulatory approval studies, testing, and product design—provided they are carried out in continuity with R&D work performed in Québec. Eligible CRIC expenditures encompass: (1) 100% of salaries and wages for R&D and pre-commercialisation in Québec; (2) capital equipment acquisition costs; and (3) 50% of subcontracting contracts (including contracts with universities, public research centres, CCTTs, or research consortia). Before applying the 30% / 20% rates, eligible expenditures are reduced by an annual Exclusion Threshold (Seuil d'exclusion) equal to the higher of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount under the Québec personal income tax regime for each eligible employee, prorated by the time that employee spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation activities. Corporations claim the CRIC on their CO-17 return (Codes 112 and 113) by filing Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures), Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)), Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (associated-group limit allocation), and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (pre-commercialisation information). (For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, claimants use the legacy Revenu Québec forms RD-1029.7-V, RD-1029.8.6-V, RD-1029.8.16.1-V, and RD-1029.8.9.03-V at the legacy 14%–30% rates.)
5.2 Ontario: Three-Credit Ecosystem (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), Ontario operates three distinct corporate R&D tax credits administered by the CRA. Following the federal enactment of Bill C-15 in March 2026, Ontario harmonized with the federal restoration of capital expenditures (allowing 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, for both the OITC and ORDTC), but kept its OITC expenditure limit at $3,000,000 and retained its existing OITC income and capital phase-out thresholds.

The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96; Schedule 566, Line 468 of Schedule 5) is an 8% fully refundable tax credit for corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years), yielding a maximum annual refund of $240,000. The $3,000,000 OITC limit is reduced by two prior-year associated-group tests that are compounded (multiplied together) rather than evaluated on a "lesser of" basis: (1) a prior-year federal taxable income grind between $500,000 and $800,000; and (2) a prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada grind between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000:

OITC Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × [($800,000 − A) ÷ $300,000] × [($50,000,000 − B) ÷ $25,000,000], where A is the prior-year taxable income and B is the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations

(Neither factor can be less than zero, and the limit cannot exceed $3,000,000; for example, with $700,000 prior-year taxable income and $30,000,000 prior-year taxable capital, the income factor yields $1,000,000 and the capital factor retains 80% [$20,000,000 ÷ $25,000,000], producing an $800,000 expenditure limit and a $64,000 maximum OITC.) A corporation may waive the OITC under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario).

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45; Schedule 508, Line 416 of Schedule 5) is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment, with no expenditure cap and no income or capital phase-outs. Under Ontario statutory ordering rules, the 8% OITC is treated as government assistance that reduces the eligible Ontario expenditure base before the 3.5% ORDTC is calculated. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 taxation years and carries forward 20 taxation years against Ontario corporate income tax payable (and may be waived in writing within 6 months of taxation year-end or on an amended return to prevent grinding the 35% federal cash refund in loss years).

The Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97; Schedules 568 and 569, Line 470 of Schedule 5) is a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario expenditures incurred under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) (Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence), subject to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20,000,000 across associated corporations (maximum annual cash refund of $4,000,000).
5.3 British Columbia: Permanent 10% Credit & Full Harmonization under B.C. Budget 2026

Under Part 6 (Sections 97 to 103) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 215, as amended by Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026, introduced February 17, 2026, passed Third Reading April 1, 2026), British Columbia made its 10% SR&ED Tax Credit permanent and fully harmonized with all federal Bill C-15 changes effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

Under section 98, qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a B.C. permanent establishment earn a 10% fully refundable credit (claimed on Form T666 and reported on Line 674 of Schedule 5) up to the federal expenditure limit—which increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (raising the maximum B.C. refundable credit from $300,000 to $600,000), subject to the broadened $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year average gross revenue) phase-out, and including restored capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024. Under section 99, all other qualifying corporations (and CCPCs/ECPCs on B.C. expenditures above their $6,000,000 limit, plus active corporate partners of a partnership under section 99.1) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Line 659 of Schedule 5), which carries back 3 taxation years and carries forward 10 taxation years (and may be renounced under section 100). Form T666 must be filed within 18 months after the end of the taxation year (section 103), and a 10-year provincial recapture rule applies under section 102.1.
5.4 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Effective January 1, 2021, under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, Alberta administers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) through Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration). The IEG provides a 100% refundable payment on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta SR&ED expenditures equal to: (1) an 8% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (defined as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D expenditures over the preceding 2 taxation years); plus (2) an enhanced 20% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's 2-year average base spending level. Grant eligibility phases out linearly for corporations with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 (corporations over $50,000,000 are ineligible). The IEG is claimed on the Alberta AT1 return using AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (21 months after taxation year-end).

body.text: 7. Comprehensive Jurisprudence & Audit Precedents
Canadian SR&ED tax administration is governed by an extensive body of binding jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
7.1 The Foundational Trilogy on Technical Eligibility & Contemporaneous Evidence

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED law is Justice Bowman's decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520 (TCC). Evaluating five physical hydraulic scale-modelling projects, the Tax Court of Canada allowed four projects and articulated the five judicial criteria for SR&ED: (1) technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; (2) formulation of hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) adoption of a procedure according with the total discipline of the scientific method, including formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses; (4) achievement of a technological advancement; and (5) keeping a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results as the work progressed. Crucially, Northwest Hydraulic established that "system uncertainty" can exist even when individual components are well known, and held that proving a hypothesis false is itself a technological advancement (a principle reinforced in Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, 96-4369-IT-G (1999 TCC)).

Shortly thereafter, the Federal Court of Appeal elevated Justice Bowman's five criteria to binding national precedent in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 CTC 132 (FCA) (reversing 96 DTC 1808 (TCC)) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA) (affirming 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC)). In RIS-Christie, involving a patented concrete damp-proofing panel where the lead engineer had died before trial, the FCA emphasized that documentary records of repeatable testing are vital because a final product or patent does not by itself prove systematic investigation, but held that credible oral testimony must still be weighed where extreme circumstances explain documentary gaps. Conversely, in C.W. Agencies, the FCA dismissed a software appeal where the claimant failed to call its project manager or developers and relied instead on an external expert witness (Dr. Slonim) who inspected the finished code post-facto and conjectured what problems must have occurred—establishing that post-facto expert conjecture cannot substitute for contemporaneous records and first-hand witness testimony (building on Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC)).
7.2 Routine Engineering vs. Experimental Development & Credibility of Evidence (2011–2021)

Between 2011 and 2021, appellate and trial rulings sharpened the boundary between routine engineering and experimental development. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (affirming 2010 TCC), the courts held that although the taxpayer maintained thorough records of testing materials for a thermoformed storage bin ("Multi-Bin"), resolving design parameters using techniques and data accessible to competent professionals in the field constitutes routine engineering, not SR&ED. Conversely, in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, and 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77, the TCC ruled in favour of the claimants despite sparse formal documentation, holding that highly credible oral testimony corroborated by contemporaneous artefacts can satisfy the evidentiary burden.

Where both technical witness testimony and contemporaneous records are absent, however, claims consistently fail: in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed appeals for a counterweight-free theatre fire curtain and a manual override system because no engineer testified and the "Experiment Summary Sheets" submitted at trial had been prepared retroactively by the external SR&ED tax consultant after the projects were completed. Similarly, in National Research and Development Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (dynamic SQL database software), Indusol Industrial Control Ltd. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 103 (marine control software), and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, the courts dismissed the claims and reaffirmed that merely identifying a problem or stating an initial hypothesis without proving a systematic experimental investigation and technological advancement fails the Northwest Hydraulic test.
7.3 Modern Jurisprudence on System Uncertainty, Software/SaaS & Food/Manufacturing R&D (2023–2026)
Recent Tax Court of Canada decisions from 2023 through 2026 provide critical guidance across software, manufacturing, energy, and food processing:

Demonstrated how complex mechanical and electronic system integration uncertainties satisfy the Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Shelf-stable vinegar-based beverage microbial control (Food Science)

Justice Bodie held that: (1) a technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution/preservative exists, provided it has never been used in the specific context; and (2) contemporaneous records do not need to be written for an uninitiated outsider to replicate, provided they track hypotheses, tests, and results for the team.

Landmark software victory: systemic uncertainty in integrating open-source tools (React/Redux) went beyond routine debugging/optimization; courts must evaluate software projects holistically rather than splintering tasks.

body.text: 7.4 Jurisprudence on Government Assistance, CCPC Control & Statutory Filing Deadlines
Finally, four major appellate lines of authority govern financial and procedural compliance:

items: Concessional Government Loans as "Government Assistance" (Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196; CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178, aff'g 2021 TCC 57): Both the TCC and the Federal Court of Appeal held that unconditionally or conditionally repayable government contributions (such as Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative [SADI] loans to CAE Inc.) constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x) because their terms are not strictly commercial arrangements motivated by an ordinary business return—meaning they both reduce the claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18) and must be included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x).

De Jure and De Facto Control for CCPC Status (Canada v. Bioartificial Gel Technologies (Bagtech) Inc., 2013 FCA, aff'g 2012 TCC; McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA; Aeronautic Development Corp. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 39): In Bagtech, the FCA confirmed that a valid Unanimous Shareholders Agreement (USA) stripping non-resident majority shareholders of the power to elect a majority of the board of directors prevented non-resident de jure control, preserving CCPC status for the 35% enhanced ITC. Conversely, in McGillivray and Aeronautic Development Corp., the courts held that undue operational or governance influence by a non-resident or public corporation establishes de facto control under subsection 256(5.1), disqualifying the company from CCPC status even where non-residents hold <50% of voting shares.

Partnership 15% ITC Restriction (All Colour Chemicals, TCC): Confirmed that the specific partnership ITC rule in subsection 127(8) overrides the CCPC enhanced rate in subsection 127(10.1), restricting corporate partners of a partnership to the 15% basic ITC rate.

Strict Enforcement of the 18-Month Reporting Deadline (Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA, aff'g 2015 TCC 211; Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA, aff'g 2017 TCC 9): In Easy Way Cattle Oilers, the taxpayer timely filed Form T661 (securing its Section 37 deduction) but filed Schedule T2SCH31 after the 18-month reporting deadline; the Federal Court of Appeal denied 100% of the ITC, holding that filing the prescribed ITC schedule by the 18-month deadline is a mandatory statutory condition precedent. In Westsource, the FCA held that project descriptions filed only by a related company did not satisfy the claimant's own 18-month filing obligation.
